The poet issues forth upon this sorry sphere, His mother, horrified, and full of blasphemy, Uplifts her voice to God, who takes compassion on her.
"Ah, why did I not bear a serpent's nest entire, Instead of bringing forth this hideous Child of Doom!
When I conceived my expiation in my womb!"
"Yet since among all women thou hast chosen me
And since I cannot like a love-leaf wantonly Consign this stunted monster to the glowing grate,"
"I'll cause thine overwhelming hatred to rebound
Forsooth, the branches of this wretched tree I'll wound And rob its pestilential blossoms of their might!"
And knowing not the changeless statutes of all times, Herself, amid the flames of hell, prepares the pyre;
Yet 'neath th' invisible shelter of an Angel's wing
Exhales from all he eats and drinks, and everything The ever sweet ambrosia and the nectar red.
He trifles with the winds and with the clouds that glide,
The spirit on his pilgrimage; that faithful guide, Oft weeps to see him joyful like a bird of Spring.
All those that he would cherish shrink from him with fear,
Endeavour hard some grievance from his heart to tear, And make on him the trial of their ferocity.
Within the bread and wine outspread for his repast
And everything he touches, forth they slyly cast, Or scourge themselves, if e'er their feet betrod his way.
His wife goes round proclaiming in the crowded quads-- "Since he can find my body beauteous to behold,
And like unto them, redeck myself with shining gold?"
"I'll bathe myself with incense, spikenard and myrrh,
To see, in jest, if from a heart, that loves me dear, I cannot filch away the hommages divine."
"And when of these impious jokes at length I tire, My frail but mighty hands, around his breast entwined, With nails, like harpies' nails, shall cunningly conspire
"And like a youngling bird that trembles in its nest, I'll pluck his heart right out; within its own blood drowned,
I'll throw it with intense disdain upon the ground!"
Towards the Heavens where he sees the sacred grail
Whereon the lightenings from his lucid spirit veil The sight of the infuriated mob that swarms.
"Oh blest be thou, Almighty who bestowest pain,
And like the most refreshing and the purest rain, To sanctify the strong, for saintly ecstasies."
"I know that for the poet thou wilt grant a chair,
That of the endless feast thou wilt accord his share To him, of Virtues, Dominations and of Thrones."
"I know, that Sorrow is that nobleness alone,
I know, in order to enwreathe my mystic crown I must inspire the ages and the universe."
"And yet the buried jewels of Palmyra old,
Of gems, that unto me you show could never hold Beside this diadem of blinding brilliancy."
"For it shall be engendered from the purest fire
Of which the eyes of Mortals, in their sheen entire, Are but the tarnished mirrors, sad and overcast!"
